cells: Use them for the evaluation
Work out suitable criteria by discussing them with senior management, the board or both

rows.label: May
cells: Suggest better criteria for the engagement
Recommend management adopt the criteria identified; assist, or seek an expert's input

rows.label: Possible outcome
cells: Assurance against the existing criteria
The discussion may lead to advisory work instead

subtopics.example: Kwame audits drug-dispensing records at a Ghanaian hospital group. The pharmacy policy says only that records must be accurate. Kwame judges this too vague to measure, so Kwame discusses criteria with the chief medical officer and the chief financial officer, who agree on a stock-count variance limit and a same-day recording rule. Kwame documents the agreed criteria and informs the pharmacy manager.

review: Evaluate each criterion against the objective it serves before testing
Compare management's measures with the stated tolerance and thresholds
Inspect the record of any discussion that replaced inadequate criteria
evidence: Minuted or written agreement on the criteria to be used
Policies or targets showing thresholds and the satisfactory level of control
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to document measurable criteria, with thresholds, for the activity's key objectives.
audit_focus.decides: Senior leaders, not the activity's own managers, settle replacement criteria

subtopics.isaca_rule: Use adequate criteria the board and senior management set; if inadequate, work out better ones with senior management, the board or both. Suggesting is not replacing.

exam_traps.trap: Adequate criteria set by the board and senior management can be swapped for the internal auditor's preferred standard.
exam_traps.why: If they are adequate, the internal auditor must use them. Better criteria may be suggested, not imposed.

exam_traps.trap: Criteria must be used simply because management set them.
exam_traps.why: Only adequate criteria must be used; inadequate ones give way to criteria worked out with the board, senior management or both.

key_terms.definition: The share of transactions or controls that must work as intended for a control process to count as acceptable.
The size of error or loss above which the organization treats a matter as significant for a unit or process.

subtopics.memory_aid: Adequate: relevant, aligned, comparable. Good: also specific and practical.

subtopics.name: Criteria in Practice: Timing, Agreement and Gaps
subtopics.definition: Settling criteria in practice means fixing them in the work program before testing, agreeing them at the right level, and telling management which ones will be used.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Criteria picked after the results are known look like a verdict in search of a rule. Agreed, documented criteria prevent disputes about findings later.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.6): the work program names the criteria for each objective, so they are set before it is approved and testing begins.
Must: where criteria are missing, work them out with senior management, the board or both, as for inadequate ones (2A2.2).
Should: inform the management of the activity of the criteria and document the agreed set, so it is not misread or challenged later.
May: recommend that management adopt the criteria the internal auditors identified, or turn the work into advisory services.
Should: research recommended practice and compare management's criteria with other organizations'; a comparison informs judgment and does not override adequate criteria.
Must: a new or changed objective needs its own criteria, approved with the revised work program.
subtopics.example: Before fieldwork on a Moroccan airline's fuel purchasing, internal auditor Youssef finds no written limit on hedging losses. Rather than test first and choose a limit later, Youssef proposes criteria based on the board's approved risk tolerance, agrees them with the chief financial officer, informs the treasury manager and records the agreement before the work program goes for approval.

review: Compare the date criteria were agreed with the date testing began
Inspect the work program for criteria named against every objective
Trace any criterion changed after testing to an approved change
evidence: Dated work program approval showing criteria for each objective
Email or minutes informing management of the criteria to be used
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management of the activity to adopt and document the agreed criteria for its own future monitoring.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a supervisor the executive delegates to, approves the work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Fix criteria before testing, agree missing ones at the right level, and tell management which ones apply.

exam_traps.trap: Test first, then choose the criteria that best explain the exceptions found.
exam_traps.why: Criteria come before testing, and the work program names them for each objective. Criteria picked to fit the results look biased and invite challenge.

exam_traps.trap: Every advisory engagement needs formal evaluation criteria.
exam_traps.why: For advisory services, identifying criteria may not be needed, depending on the agreement with the relevant stakeholders.

key_terms.definition: A comparison point from another unit or organization; it informs a judgment but is not automatically a criterion.
Criteria shared with management and recorded before testing, so findings are measured against a known yardstick.

topics.topic_name: Planning around key risks and controls
topics.overview: Planning draws on business knowledge at recognize level: the activity's strategy and measures, cybersecurity and IT controls, readiness for disruption, finance basics, and the key risks of common processes and systems, with the Topical Requirements as a baseline. The aim is to spot the risk and the kind of control, not to configure or calculate.
can_do: Plan an engagement around the activity's strategic objectives and the measures management uses
Recognize cyber, IT, privacy and data security risks and the controls that commonly address them
Recognize continuity, recovery and resilience ideas that shape an engagement's risks
Recognize finance terms and the main risks of common business processes and systems

subtopics.name: Strategy, Performance Measures and Topical Requirements in Planning
subtopics.definition: Planning around strategy means starting from what the activity is trying to achieve, how its risks are managed and how management measures and manages its performance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Risks matter because they threaten objectives. Starting from strategy and measures aims the engagement at what leaders care about, not at what is easiest to test.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.2): learn the strategy, objectives and risks that bear on the activity, and the criteria management uses to judge progress.
Sound practice: trace the chain from a strategic objective to the risks to it, then to the measures and targets that show whether it is on track.
Performance measures such as key performance indicators (KPIs) are often usable criteria; performance management is whether management reviews them and acts.
Sound practice: look for measures that reward one result while pushing risk elsewhere, such as a sales target that weakens credit checks.
Must: a Topical Requirement in scope is the minimum; map its governance, risk management and controls requirements to the risk assessment, criteria and work program steps.
subtopics.example: A Danish hospital group's strategy is to cut emergency waiting times, tracked only by average wait. Planning an engagement on emergency care, internal auditor Mette notes that nothing measures whether faster triage misses serious cases, and that ward bonuses depend on the average. Mette adds patient safety risk to the engagement risk assessment and plans to ask how missed diagnoses are tracked.

review: Compare engagement objectives with the goals in the activity's business plan
Map each key risk to a measure that would reveal it
Sample performance reports for follow-up on missed targets
evidence: Strategy and business plan for the activity under review
Performance reports with targets, results and management's responses
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to add measures that track the main risks to each strategic objective, not only output.
audit_focus.decides: Management sets the activity's measures; the board oversees strategy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Plan from the activity's objectives outward: strategy, the risks to it, then the measures management uses. A Topical Requirement in scope is the floor.

exam_traps.trap: Planning starts from the list of controls management provides.
exam_traps.why: Planning starts from objectives and risks. Controls are judged by whether they manage the risks to the activity's objectives.

exam_traps.trap: A measure that is on target proves the risks are managed.
exam_traps.why: Targets show results, not risk. A measure can be met while risk builds elsewhere, so planning looks at how measures and risks connect.

key_terms.definition: A high-level goal an organization or activity sets in order to carry out its strategy.
A measure management uses to track progress toward an objective, such as on-time delivery.
How management sets targets, reviews results and acts on them.

subtopics.memory_aid: Objective, risk, measure: plan along that chain.

subtopics.name: Cybersecurity, IT Controls and Data Protection
subtopics.definition: Cybersecurity protects systems, networks and data from attack and misuse; it is part of information security, which keeps information confidential, accurate and available.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Most processes run on technology, so cyber and IT weaknesses can defeat business controls; the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement sets a mandatory baseline and is testable now.
how_it_works: Must: for cyber assurance, assess the requirement's three parts: governance, risk management (incident response and recovery included) and controls such as access, patching, encryption and network security.
Threats named in The IIA's user guides include ransomware, malware, denial of service, data breaches, phishing and insider threats.
Must: assess whether management continuously monitors emerging threats, and whether vendors' controls protect the organization's systems and data.
Should: map planned cyber tests to the requirement; an IT control framework such as NIST's helps coverage, but adopting one does not prove controls work.
Must (Standard 5.2): follow the privacy laws and policies that apply; planning asks what personal data is held, where, who can reach it and why.
Knowledge (NIST Privacy Framework; SP 800-53 PT-3): strong security does not settle privacy; harm can come from the organization's own use of personal data beyond its collected purpose.
subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on a Polish supermarket chain's grocery orders, internal auditor Kasia sees customer addresses and payment details passing through a vendor's platform. Kasia assesses the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement for applicability, plans to review the vendor's assurance report and the chain's access controls, and records why governance items are excluded: the risk lies in how controls are run.

review: Inspect the applicability record against each Cybersecurity Topical Requirement section
Compare system user lists with current staff and their roles
Inspect vendor assurance reports for scope, period and exceptions
evidence: System-generated user access listings with last review dates
Vendor service organization control (SOC) reports covering the period
Patch and vulnerability reports from security tools
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the chief information security officer to report access review and patching exceptions to management each quarter.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns cyber controls; the board oversees the cyber strategy

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize the risk and the kind of control; never configure it. A framework adopted is not a control proven.

exam_traps.trap: An automatic system check that rejects an invoice with no matching purchase order is an IT general control.
exam_traps.why: In common usage, a check built into one system's processing is an application control; IT general controls cover the whole environment, such as access, change and operations.

key_terms.definition: Common usage: controls over the whole IT environment, such as access, change and operations, that every system relies on.
Common usage: controls built into one system's processing, such as input checks and automatic matching.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-53 CM-3, AC-5): proposed changes are reviewed and approved first; duties are split so no one misuses a privilege unchecked.

subtopics.name: Continuity, Recovery and Resilience Readiness
subtopics.definition: Readiness for disruption is an organization's ability to keep critical services going and recover after a crisis, through continuity plans, recovery plans, incident response and tests.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Disruption is when untested plans fail. Recognizing whether recovery has been proven, not just written down, shows where an engagement's real risk sits.
how_it_works: A business continuity plan keeps critical work going in a disaster; a disaster recovery plan restores IT systems, data and operations afterward.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-34): a business impact analysis sets each process's maximum tolerable downtime; a supporting system's recovery time objective is normally shorter, leaving time to catch up.
Incident response covers detection, prioritization, containment, recovery and a post-incident review that feeds future plans.
Sound practice: treat backups as unproven until data is restored; the resilience user guide links recovery objectives to restore testing.
Must (resilience requirement, effective April 2027, on the exam from October 2027): assess whether plans are tested, as in tabletop rehearsals, and results go to the board and senior management.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-34): the recovery time objective caps downtime, checked by timed restores; the recovery point objective caps data loss, checked by how often backups run.
subtopics.example: At a Thai hospital, the IT manager reports that nightly backups of patient records always complete. Planning a continuity engagement, internal auditor Somchai asks when data was last restored and how long it took. No restore has been tried in two years, so Somchai rates recovery a significant risk and plans to review the recovery plan and tests.

review: Inspect restore test results against the recovery time objective
Compare the systems restored first with the services ranked most critical
Trace issues from the last tabletop exercise to completed actions
evidence: Restore test logs with dates, systems and times achieved
Business impact analysis ranking critical services
Exercise reports and the action tracker that followed
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to schedule restore tests for critical systems and report results against recovery objectives.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the plans; the board receives test results

subtopics.isaca_rule: Written plans and completed backups do not prove readiness; tested recovery, ranked by impact and reported upward, does.

exam_traps.trap: Nightly backups that complete successfully show the organization can recover.
exam_traps.why: A backup never restored is unproven; readiness shows in restore tests measured against the recovery objectives.

exam_traps.trap: Continuity planning is an IT matter only.
exam_traps.why: Continuity covers people, sites, suppliers and money as well as systems.

key_terms.definition: Knowledge (NIST SP 800-34): a study linking a system to the processes it supports and what their disruption would cost.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-34): the longest a system can stay down before the harm becomes unacceptable.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-34): how much recent data may be lost, set by the point the latest backup restores.

subtopics.name: Finance Basics and Business Process Risks
subtopics.definition: Recognize-level business knowledge means knowing the main financial terms and the key risks of common processes well enough to spot what an engagement must cover.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An internal auditor who cannot tell an asset from a liability, or see why ordering and paying are kept apart, misses the risks that matter during planning.
how_it_works: Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 5.3, 12.1): current means turning to cash, used or due within a year; a long loan's installment due this year is a current liability.
Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 5.3): bonds or shares management intends to hold beyond a year are long-term investments, even if they could be sold sooner.
Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 6.2): a perpetual system updates stock with every transaction, yet still needs a physical count, since theft, damage and loss leave records and shelves apart.
Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 8.3): ordering, receiving and paying sit with different people, so no one person can order, accept and pay for goods alone.
In an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, user roles decide who can do what, so access rights carry the risk of conflicting duties.
Must (Third-Party Topical Requirement, testable March 2027): for vendors prioritized by risk, assess management's offboarding plan: access revoked, data returned or destroyed.

rows.label: Current assets
cells: Cash, or items turned into cash or used within about a year
Real, collectable, safe?

rows.label: Long-term assets
cells: Fixed assets such as buildings and equipment, and investments meant to be held beyond a year
Recorded, protected, valued properly?

rows.label: Short-term liabilities
cells: Amounts due within about a year, a long loan's current installment included
All recorded and paid on time?

rows.label: Long-term liabilities
cells: Obligations due later, such as long loans
Loan conditions met and reported?

rows.label: Capital
cells: Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 2.2, 14.4): equity, not a debt; contributed capital is what owners pay in for shares, kept apart from retained earnings, the profits kept
Recorded as equity, not as a loan?

types.meaning: Fictitious suppliers; duplicate or unapproved payments.
Loss, obsolete stock, reliance on one supplier.
Lost or unrecorded equipment, IT assets included.
Breaches of laws, regulations or contracts.
Customer (CRM), transaction (ERP) and risk (GRC) systems: personal data, conflicting access, unreliable records.

subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on spare-parts purchasing at a Chilean copper mine, internal auditor Diego learns that one buyer can create suppliers, raise orders and release payments in the ERP system. Diego recognizes a high risk of payments to fictitious suppliers and plans tests of supplier set-up and access rights.

review: Compare ERP user roles with incompatible duties across purchase to payment
Trace a sample of payments to orders and receiving records
evidence: System-generated role and access reports from the ERP system
Supplier master file change log with approver names
audit_focus.recommend: Ask the procurement and finance managers to remove conflicting access and require independent approval of supplier changes.
audit_focus.decides: Process owners decide how duties are split; risk above appetite goes up the line

subtopics.isaca_rule: Recognize the term, its typical risk and the kind of control expected; management owns the process.

exam_traps.trap: One approval on each payment makes the purchasing process safe.
exam_traps.why: Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 8.3): ordering, receiving and paying sit with different people. A later approval that relies on the buyer's own order and delivery records does not restore that split.

key_terms.definition: Common usage: matching the purchase order, the receiving record and the supplier invoice before paying.
Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one can make and hide an error or fraud alone.
Knowledge (OpenStax Accounting 5.3): current assets divided by current liabilities, a simple sign of whether debts due within the year can be met.

subtopics.memory_aid: Order, receive, pay: three people, one match.

topics.overview: An engagement can be run in different ways: traditional, agile, integrated or remote. This topic covers what each offers, how to choose by objectives, risk and resources, and the project management ideas that keep an engagement on time and on budget. The Standards' musts apply whatever the approach.
can_do: Evaluate traditional, agile, integrated and remote ways of working for a given engagement
Determine which approach fits the objectives, risks, deadline and resources
Describe how scope, schedule, time budget and staffing are run like a project

subtopics.name: Traditional, Agile, Integrated and Remote Approaches
subtopics.definition: An engagement approach is the way the work is organized and delivered: in fixed stages, in short repeated cycles, joined up across disciplines, or from a distance.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The approach changes speed, cost and how often management sees results, but never the Standards. A newer approach is not permission to skip a requirement.
how_it_works: Must: every approach keeps documented objectives and scope, criteria, an approved work program, sufficient evidence, supervision and documentation.
Must: in agile work too, each work program change is approved by the chief audit executive (CAE) or a supervisor the CAE delegates to.
Must: remote evidence is still relevant, reliable and sufficient (Standard 14.1), so plan how to obtain it first-hand.
Sound practice: integration needs the right mix of skills on one team, or specialists working to the same objectives under the same supervision.

types.meaning: Planning, fieldwork and reporting in sequence, with results mostly at the end. Predictable, but issues surface late.
Short cycles of planning, testing and feedback, with priorities adjusted as results arrive. Suits fast-changing areas; needs frequent contact.
Joining in one engagement what the objectives need, from objectives and scope to techniques, staffing and reporting, for example process, IT and finance work together.
Work done away from the site through system access, video and shared files. Saves travel; observation and inspection get harder.

subtopics.example: Rangi leads an engagement on a new mobile payments app at an Australian credit union that releases updates every two weeks. Rangi proposes an agile approach: two-week testing cycles, an IT specialist on the team and a short results meeting with the product owner after each cycle. The engagement supervisor approves the work program for the first cycle, and each revision before it runs.

review: Compare the chosen approach with the objectives, risks and deadline
Confirm no cycle's testing started before its plan was approved
Sample remote evidence for its source, date and how it was obtained
evidence: Planning memo explaining why the approach was chosen
Approved work program versions for each cycle or stage
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team record in the planning memo why the approach fits the objectives and risks.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive stays accountable, even when a supervisor approves

subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose the way of working that fits and keep every must. Agile changes timing, remote changes location, and neither lowers the evidence bar.

exam_traps.trap: Agile auditing means skipping a formal work program to move faster.
exam_traps.why: The work program must still be documented and approved before it is carried out, and promptly after changes; agile changes the timing, not that rule.

exam_traps.trap: An integrated engagement is simply another name for an IT audit.
exam_traps.why: Integration combines what the objectives need, such as process, finance and IT work, the staff and the reporting, into one engagement; it is not about IT alone.

key_terms.definition: How an engagement's work is organized and delivered, chosen to fit its objectives, risks and resources.
The chief audit executive's documented way of working, which internal auditors follow.

subtopics.memory_aid: The approach changes how and when, never the musts.

subtopics.name: Choosing the Approach That Fits
subtopics.definition: Choosing an approach means weighing the engagement's objectives, risks, complexity, deadline, stakeholders and resources, then picking the way of working that serves them best.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A choice made out of habit wastes effort or misses risk. Matching the approach to the job lets the team deliver reliable results when stakeholders need them.
how_it_works: Sound practice: start from the objectives and the significant risks: what must be shown, to whom and by when.
Knowledge (OpenStax Information Systems 9.1): a predictive plan suits fixed, well-defined goals; an adaptive approach repeats short planning cycles to absorb requirements that keep changing.
Must (Standard 13.5 Engagement Resources): consider the engagement's nature and complexity, its time frame, and whether money, people and technology are enough.
Should: weigh constraints such as hours budgeted, timing, travel and work in several languages.
Must: follow the chief audit executive's (CAE's) methodologies, which set how engagements are performed (Standard 9.3).
Should: where a risk needs physical inspection or observation, plan a site visit even within a remote approach, since first-hand evidence is more reliable.

rows.label: Fast-changing subject, early results wanted
cells: Agile
Approval of each work program revision

rows.label: Stable process, fixed reporting date
cells: Traditional
Issues surfacing late

rows.label: Risks spanning process, IT and finance
cells: Integrated
The right mix of skills under one supervision

rows.label: Scattered sites, data held centrally
cells: Remote
Risks that still need inspection on site

subtopics.example: Amara must review cash handling at forty small branches of a Nigerian microfinance bank within six weeks. Transaction data sits in one central system, but cash counts need someone on site. Amara plans a remote analysis of every branch's data to rank them, then surprise cash counts at the eight highest-risk branches, and explains the choice to the engagement supervisor.

review: Evaluate whether the planning memo ties the approach to objectives and risks
Compare budgeted hours and dates with what the approach demands
Inspect evidence plans for risks that need work on site
evidence: Planning memo with the approach and its reasons
Time and cost budget for the engagement
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead confirm the planning memo gives a reason for the approach before the work program is approved.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a supervisor the executive delegates to, approves the approach

subtopics.isaca_rule: Choose by objectives, risk and resources, not habit or novelty, and keep first-hand evidence where the risk needs it.

exam_traps.trap: Use last year's approach so the results are comparable.
exam_traps.why: Comparability is one factor. The approach must fit this engagement's objectives, risks, deadline and resources.

exam_traps.trap: Working remotely justifies accepting scanned copies in place of the inspection the risk needs.
exam_traps.why: Evidence must still be relevant, reliable and sufficient. If the risk needs inspection or observation, plan it, or treat the gap as a limit on the work.

key_terms.definition: What the engagement examines and how hard it is, which drive the skills, time and methods it needs.
A limit on how the work can be done, such as hours, timing, travel or language.

subtopics.name: Project Management in an Engagement
subtopics.definition: Project management in an engagement means running it like a project: a defined scope, a schedule, a time budget, assigned people, progress tracking and controlled changes.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Engagements that drift miss reporting dates and overrun budgets, and stakeholders stop trusting the function. The IIA's Competency Framework lists project management among internal auditors' professional skills.
how_it_works: Knowledge (OpenStax Information Systems 9.2): once scope is set, a work breakdown structure splits it into tasks small enough to estimate and order; the schedule is built from them.
Should: set the timeline and assign staff by the work program's steps and the hours each needs (Standard 13.5).
Must (Standard 13.6 Work Program): the work program names the internal auditor assigned to each task.
Must: a supervisor guides the team and checks the work program is complete (Standard 12.3). May: compare actual with budgeted hours afterward.
Must: changes to objectives, scope or the work program are approved, like changes to any project baseline.
Should: agree with management at the start how often updates will come and who receives the final communication.
subtopics.example: Sofia supervises a six-week inventory engagement at an Italian fashion house. Sofia splits the work program into tasks, each with hours and an owner, sets weekly check-ins with the warehouse director and tracks hours used against the budget. When stock counts take longer than planned in week three, Sofia raises the overrun with the chief audit executive instead of dropping planned steps.

review: Compare budgeted and actual hours by task at engagement close
Inspect the work program for an owner and target date per task
Trace each schedule slip to a documented decision
evidence: Timesheets showing hours charged to each task
Status reports or meeting notes shared with management
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead compare hours used with the budget each week and report slips early.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides on extra time or staff

subtopics.isaca_rule: Run the engagement like a project: approved scope, schedule, hours, named owners and controlled changes. Overruns go up, never into dropped steps.

exam_traps.trap: When fieldwork runs late, cut the lowest-risk steps without telling anyone.
exam_traps.why: Dropping planned steps changes the work program, and perhaps the scope; both need approval, and resource problems go to the chief audit executive.

key_terms.definition: The hours planned for each task, used to schedule staff and track progress.
A planned point in the schedule, such as the end of fieldwork, used to check progress.
Comparing the hours used with the hours planned, during or after the engagement.
Knowledge (OpenStax Information Systems 9.2): the work split into smaller tasks, the basis for estimates, their order and the schedule.

subtopics.memory_aid: Scope, schedule, hours, owners, tracking, change control.

topics.overview: The engagement risk assessment turns planning information into a ranked list of risks that drives the objectives, scope and tests. This topic covers completing it: applying Topical Requirements, pervasive and emerging risks, the effect of change, structure and culture, and the methods used to rate and rank risks and controls.
can_do: Complete an engagement risk assessment that identifies, rates and ranks the activity's risks, fraud included
Recognize pervasive and emerging risks and how change, structure and culture shift them
Determine suitable methods and yardsticks to rank risks and pick the controls worth testing
Apply a Topical Requirement's applicability check, using the guidance's risk test to decide which parts apply

subtopics.name: Completing the Engagement Risk Assessment
subtopics.definition: Completing the engagement risk assessment means turning what was learned about the activity into a documented, ranked list of significant risks, fraud included, and their intended controls.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Everything after it rests on this step. A risk left off the list is never tested, and a wrongly ranked one takes time from the risks that matter.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.2 Engagement Risk Assessment): understand how the activity is meant to work, identify the potentially significant risks to its objectives, consider fraud, and prioritize by significance.
Must: the plan's risk assessment is one input, never the engagement's own (see 1C2.2).
Must: where past engagements identified the relevant risks, review and update that assessment; reusing it unchanged does not meet the requirement.

Should: weigh management's input, but judge significance yourself. Must (Third-Party Topical Requirement, testable March 2027): the organization stays accountable for risks to its objectives when vendors do the work.
May: for advisory work, skip the formal written assessment if the agreement with stakeholders allows.

Should (Application Guidance, not a Standard): when a Topical Requirement's topic surfaces, rate its inherent risk by impact and likelihood; above the critical threshold, apply the matching requirements.
subtopics.example: Planning a second engagement on grant payments at a Kenyan development agency, internal auditor Achieng starts from the assessment done three years ago. Achieng updates it for a new online application portal, a cut in finance staff and a donor's alert about fake grantees, adds and ranks the new risks, fraud among them, and sends the result to the engagement supervisor.

review: Compare the assessment's date and inputs with changes since the last engagement
Confirm fraud risks were identified and ranked with the others
Trace each significant risk to an objective and a planned test
evidence: Dated engagement risk assessment with ratings and reasons
Notes of planning discussions with management and the supervisor
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team date and initial each review of an earlier engagement risk assessment before reusing it.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a supervisor the executive delegates to, approves the resulting scope

subtopics.isaca_rule: Build the engagement's own ranked list of significant risks, fraud included; earlier assessments are updated, and management's view is input, not the answer.

exam_traps.trap: Last cycle's engagement risk assessment can be reused unchanged.
exam_traps.why: Where past engagements identified the risks, a review and update is enough, but it is required: changes since then may add or re-rank risks.

exam_traps.trap: Management's own risk register can replace the engagement risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Management's assessment can help identify risks, but the internal auditor must assess and rank the activity's risks, judging significance independently.

key_terms.definition: The planning step that identifies and ranks the risks of the activity being examined.
In the Topical Requirements Application Guidance, the level of risk, tied to risk appetite, above which a topic counts as significant.

subtopics.name: Pervasive and Emerging Risks
subtopics.definition: Pervasive risks run through a whole activity, not one step, such as financial, operational, IT, cyber and regulatory risk; emerging risks are new or changing, with little history.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A risk assessment built step by step can miss risks that touch every step, and last year's data misses what is new.
how_it_works: Pervasive means present across the activity: a weak system or a new regulation touches every process that uses it or falls under it.
Must (Standard 13.2): consider fraud risk in every engagement risk assessment; Standard 3.1's considerations call fraud a pervasive risk.
Should: consider cyber risk when planning, scoping and carrying out most assurance engagements, not only cyber ones (Cybersecurity user guide).
Emerging risks include new technology such as artificial intelligence, new regulation, market shifts and slow-building pressures that are easy to overlook.
Sound practice: rate emerging risks, which have little loss history, by judgment, scenarios and outside sources such as regulators and threat intelligence.
subtopics.example: Planning an engagement on the claims process at a Dutch health insurer, internal auditor Sanne lists step-level risks such as duplicate claims. Sanne then adds risks that cut across every step: weak change controls in the claims system, a national data law starting next year, and a plan to let an artificial intelligence tool approve small claims.

review: Compare the risk list with risks that span every process step
Inspect planning notes for regulatory and technology changes due soon
Evaluate whether new risks were rated low only for lack of losses
evidence: Regulatory change calendar or compliance team updates
Industry or threat reports used in rating
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to add emerging risks, with owners and review dates, to the activity's risk register.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the risk register and the responses to emerging risks

subtopics.isaca_rule: Look across the activity as well as along it, and rate new risks by judgment, not by their missing loss history.

exam_traps.trap: A risk with no losses to date can be rated low.
exam_traps.why: Emerging risks have little history. Their rating rests on judgment and outside information about likelihood and impact, not on past losses.

exam_traps.trap: IT risk belongs only in IT engagements.
exam_traps.why: Most processes run on systems, so IT and cyber risks are pervasive and are considered when planning engagements on business processes too.

key_terms.definition: A risk present across an activity or organization, such as fraud or system failure.
A new or fast-changing risk with little history, whose likelihood and impact are still uncertain.
Information about current and likely attacks, used to anticipate cyber risk.

subtopics.name: Change, Structure and Culture as Risk Factors
subtopics.definition: Change, structure and culture are conditions around an activity, such as new people or systems, how decisions are spread and how people behave, that move its risks.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Controls are designed for a setting. When people, systems or structure change, or culture rewards the wrong things, working controls can quietly fail.
how_it_works: Sound practice: rate risk higher after change in people (turnover, reliance on one person), processes (new steps, outsourcing) or systems (new or migrated software).
Structure and work setting move where risk gathers and review happens; the table shows what to ask.
May: use organizational charts and job descriptions to see who is responsible, then confirm it through interviews and walk-throughs (Standard 13.2).
Must (Organizational Behavior Topical Requirement, on the exam from June 2027): assess how the organization spots and corrects recurring behavior patterns, not just one-off cases.
Must (same): assess both halves of the tone control: clear, consistent expectations through reachable channels, and structured feedback showing staff understand and support them.
Must (same): assess whether behavior monitoring is timely and its results reported. Example only (user guide): decisions made without effective challenge signal behavioral risk.

rows.label: Centralized
cells: One system, team or leader, which can become a single point of failure
Is there backup, and independent review at the center?

rows.label: Decentralized
cells: Local practices and reliance on local leaders
Do policies apply everywhere, and do local issues reach head office?

rows.label: Flat structure
cells: Wide spans of control with fewer reviewers
Who reviews and approves, and is that person independent of the work?

rows.label: Traditional layers
cells: Many approval steps that can slow escalation
Do urgent issues and bad news travel up quickly?

rows.label: Remote or hybrid work
cells: Access, devices and supervision at a distance
How are work, access and approvals monitored?

subtopics.example: A Peruvian food exporter has moved its regional offices into one shared service center and removed a layer of supervisors. Planning an engagement on export documents, auditor Lucia notes a new system, staff new to the work and approvals now given by one team lead, so Lucia raises the rating for document errors and plans to test who reviews each shipment.

review: Compare charts and job descriptions with who actually approves
Inspect records of new systems, processes or staff during the period
Evaluate whether incentives reward behavior that works against controls
evidence: Organization charts before and after the change
Staff turnover and vacancy figures for the activity
Themes from employee surveys or speak-up channels
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to reassess the activity's risks and controls whenever people, processes, systems or structure change significantly.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the change and its controls; the board oversees culture

subtopics.isaca_rule: A control built for yesterday's setting may not fit today's; recheck risk after change and confirm where decisions are really made.

exam_traps.trap: If the policy manual is unchanged, a reorganization does not affect the risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Controls depend on who does the work and where; a new structure, system or team can leave a written control undone.

exam_traps.trap: Culture is a soft topic outside a process engagement's risk assessment.
exam_traps.why: Culture shapes the control environment beneath every process. Tone, incentives and willingness to speak up raise or lower risk in the activity under review.

key_terms.definition: Reliance on one person whose absence would stop or weaken a process or a control.
What people visibly do at work and how they deal with one another; culture adds the drivers, such as incentives and shared values.

subtopics.memory_aid: People, process, systems, structure, culture: any change, recheck the controls.

subtopics.name: Rating and Ranking Risks and Controls
subtopics.definition: Rating and ranking means scoring each identified risk, usually by impact and likelihood, then ordering the risks and their key controls so testing goes where it matters most.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Time is limited. A ranking built on evidence and the organization's own thresholds keeps the engagement on significant risks instead of easy tests.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.2): evaluate each risk's significance and prioritize. Should: estimate it from impact, likelihood and possibly other factors, often on a heat map.
Should: use the organization's own yardsticks where they exist: risk appetite, risk tolerance and materiality thresholds for the unit or process.
Should: judge significance in context; a risk small for the organization can be significant for the activity under review (Standard 4.2).
Sound practice: rate inherent risk before counting controls, then judge the controls (definitions in 1C4.3).
May: for the most significant risks, assess control design first to decide which controls to test for operating effectiveness.
May: record each risk, its control and type, cause, effect and residual risk in a risk and control matrix.
subtopics.example: Internal auditor Farida plans an engagement on cash collection at an Egyptian toll-road operator. Farida scores six risks for impact and likelihood, setting the impact bands from the board's loss tolerance. Skimming at manual lanes scores highest, so Farida plans to judge the design of the lane cash controls first and test the sound ones in depth.

review: Compare risk ratings with the organization's stated thresholds and tolerance
Inspect whether inherent ratings were set before controls were counted
Trace the top-ranked risks to the most extensive planned tests
evidence: Heat map or rating sheet with defined scoring scales
Risk and control matrix with control types and design notes
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to define materiality thresholds for the activity where none exist.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a supervisor the executive delegates to, approves the resulting work program

subtopics.isaca_rule: Rank by impact and likelihood against the organization's thresholds, never by ease of testing; inherent first, then controls.

exam_traps.trap: Put first the risks that are quickest to test, to show progress early.
exam_traps.why: Priority follows significance, judged by impact and likelihood. Easy tests on minor risks leave the significant ones under-tested.

exam_traps.trap: Score the risk after counting the controls and record it as inherent risk.
exam_traps.why: Inherent risk is rated before controls; counting them first hides how much the activity depends on controls that may fail.

key_terms.definition: A grid plotting risks by likelihood and impact so the most significant stand out.
A control that a significant risk mainly depends on.
A working table that lines up objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage them.

subtopics.memory_aid: Impact and likelihood, against the organization's own thresholds.

topics.overview: The work program turns planning into tasks. This topic covers procedures that judge control design, tests of effectiveness and efficiency, test methods for finance, IT, operations and cybersecurity, and how to judge whether a work program is good enough to approve.
can_do: Determine procedures that judge a control's design before or alongside tests of its operation
Identify tests of effectiveness and of efficiency, and tell the two apart
Evaluate whether a work program meets the Standards and is ready for approval
Identify test methods that suit finance, IT, operations or cybersecurity objectives

subtopics.name: Procedures to Judge Control Design
subtopics.definition: A design procedure asks whether a control, performed as intended, would manage its risk: acting at the right point, by the right person, with the right information and follow-up.
subtopics.why_it_matters: You met design and operation in 1C8.1; Part 2 adds the procedures. Faithful performance of a badly designed control gives false comfort.
how_it_works: Sound practice: walk a transaction through the process to see where the control acts and what its performer actually sees.
Sound practice: compare each control with its risk in the risk and control matrix: does it prevent or detect the event, and early enough?
Sound practice: inspect the procedures, system settings and reports the control relies on, and ask what happens to exceptions.
May: judge design at planning, as a separate stage, or alongside tests of effectiveness; the timing depends on the engagement (Standard 13.6).
Should: document the design evaluation in the work program or a separate workpaper.
Must: note a design gap as a potential finding (Standard 14.2). Sound practice: size its effect rather than fully test faithful performance.
subtopics.example: At a Vietnamese garment maker, the work program calls for testing a monthly review of overtime. Internal auditor Thao first walks through the review and finds the manager sees only total hours, not hours per worker, so excessive shifts cannot show up. Thao records a design gap and proposes to the engagement supervisor an analysis of overtime per worker in place of the planned sample.

review: Confirm each key control's design was judged, at planning or alongside its operating test
Trace design gaps to potential findings rather than operating tests
evidence: Screenshots or copies of the reports the performer relies on
Design evaluation workpaper linked to the risk and control matrix
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to redesign the control so the reviewer sees the data needed to catch the risk.
audit_focus.decides: Management owns the control and decides how to redesign it

subtopics.isaca_rule: Ask whether a control could work before relying on proof that it was done; design can be judged at planning or alongside the tests.

exam_traps.trap: Sample sixty instances first; the design can be judged from the results.
exam_traps.why: Faithful performance cannot show that a control is able to catch the risk. Judge design at planning or alongside the tests; a flawed design makes full operating tests poor value (Standard 4.2).

key_terms.definition: Whether a control, performed as written, would keep its risk at an acceptable level.
Following one transaction from start to finish to see how the process really works.

subtopics.name: Testing Effectiveness and Efficiency
subtopics.definition: Effectiveness tests show whether a control worked as designed over the period; efficiency tests show whether it costs no more time or money than the risk warrants.
subtopics.why_it_matters: Both questions are in the syllabus. Confusing them, or accepting a manager's word as proof, leads to conclusions the evidence cannot carry.
how_it_works: Knowledge (ISA 500 A23, A24, A33): a test of a control looks for signs it was performed, such as dated approvals; reperforming redoes it, recalculating only checks arithmetic.
Must (Standard 14.1): weigh reliability; inquiry alone is weak, as the performer's answer comes from the person under review, not an independent source, and is uncorroborated.
Should: when sampling, the work program records the method, population, sample size and whether results can be projected.
Knowledge (ISA 500 A63 to A66): test every item, chosen items or a sample; results on items chosen for size or risk cannot be projected to the rest.
Sound practice: test efficiency by comparing a control's cost and time with the risk, and looking for duplicate controls and manual steps a system could do.
A chance to improve efficiency is a legitimate potential finding (Standard 14.2).

rows.label: Question
cells: Did the control work, every time, over the period?
Is its cost in time and money proportionate to the risk?

rows.label: Typical methods
cells: Reperform, inspect, observe, confirm, analyze all the data
Time and cost the steps, map overlapping controls

rows.label: Typical potential finding
cells: Control skipped, or exceptions not followed up
Duplicate, excessive or slow controls

subtopics.example: Testing a three-signature approval of travel claims at a Swiss foundation, internal auditor Nora reperforms the approval on claims drawn from all twelve months and finds it always done. Nora also times the process: claims under 100 francs take three weeks and cost more to approve than they are worth. Nora records the control as effective but inefficient for small claims.

review: Inspect whether samples span the whole period under review
Inspect conclusions resting only on interviews for corroborating evidence
Evaluate whether efficiency work weighed cost against the risk managed
evidence: Reperformance results and exception lists
Data analysis scripts and full-population outputs
audit_focus.recommend: Ask management to remove or merge duplicate controls once the remaining control is shown to manage the risk.
audit_focus.decides: Management decides which controls to keep, merge or remove

subtopics.isaca_rule: Prove effectiveness with evidence beyond inquiry, drawn from across the period; judge efficiency by cost against the risk.

exam_traps.trap: The process owner said in an interview that the control runs daily, so it is effective.
exam_traps.why: Inquiry alone comes from the person under review and is uncorroborated. Effectiveness needs evidence such as inspection, reperformance or data analysis.

exam_traps.trap: Testing one week in detail shows how the control worked all year.
exam_traps.why: A narrow window says little about the rest of the period. Sample across the period, or test the full population.

key_terms.definition: The internal auditor carrying out the control again to see whether it gives the right result.
How test items are chosen, from which population, how many, and whether the results can be projected.

subtopics.memory_aid: Effective: did it work? Efficient: at what cost?

subtopics.name: Judging Whether the Work Program Is Adequate
subtopics.definition: An adequate work program is the documented, approved plan of tasks that would achieve every engagement objective, built on the planning work and the engagement risk assessment.
subtopics.why_it_matters: The work program links planning to fieldwork. A gap here, such as a missing criterion or owner, becomes a gap in evidence and conclusions later.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.6): base it on the planning information, including the engagement risk assessment's results where one was done.
Must: it names, for each objective, the criteria, the tasks, the methods and tools (analytical procedures included) and the internal auditor assigned.
Must: it is approved by the chief audit executive (CAE) or a supervisor the CAE delegates to, before it is carried out and promptly after any change.
Should: approve it when it achieves the objectives efficiently, the considerations' main test (Standard 12.3).
Should: leave room to record who did each step, when, and its review, and cross-reference the planning workpapers.
Should: for advisory work, develop it together with the stakeholders who asked for the service.
subtopics.example: Engagement supervisor Tariq reviews a draft work program for a Jordanian telecom's roaming revenue engagement. Every objective has tasks, but the revenue completeness objective names no criterion and two tasks have no assigned auditor. Tariq sends it back, and fieldwork waits until a corrected version is approved.

review: Compare the draft work program with the methodology's required elements
Compare the approval date with the date fieldwork began
Trace each significant risk to at least one task
evidence: Approved work program showing dates and approver
Approved change records for later revisions
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead hold fieldwork until the work program approval is recorded.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive stays accountable, even when a supervisor approves

subtopics.isaca_rule: No fieldwork before approval: criteria, tasks, methods, tools and an assigned auditor for each objective, and every change approved promptly.

exam_traps.trap: Fieldwork can start while the work program waits for approval, as long as it is approved before the report.
exam_traps.why: The CAE or a supervisor the CAE delegates to must approve the work program before it is carried out.

exam_traps.trap: Once approved, the work program cannot change.
exam_traps.why: It changes when the work shows the need; each change, added analysis included, is approved promptly by the CAE or a supervisor the CAE delegates to.

key_terms.definition: The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.
Dated initials or an electronic approval showing who completed or reviewed a workpaper.

subtopics.memory_aid: Criteria, tasks, methods and tools, people; approved before fieldwork.

subtopics.name: Test Methods by Subject Area
subtopics.definition: Test methods are the procedures chosen to gather evidence, and the usual mix differs by subject: accounting and finance, IT systems, business operations or cybersecurity.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A generalist internal auditor is expected to recognize which method suits which subject. Choosing a method because it is familiar, not because it answers the objective, weakens the evidence.
how_it_works: Knowledge (ISA 500 A18 to A24): finance tests inspect records or assets, confirm with outside parties, recalculate and reperform; seeing an asset shows it exists, not necessarily who owns it.
May (IT systems): extract data directly from systems, inspect user lists and settings to see how controls are configured, and review change records.
Knowledge (NIST SP 800-53A): examine reviews settings and records, interview asks people, and test makes a mechanism act under set conditions; only a test shows how it behaves.
May (business operations): observe and walk through the process, compare nonfinancial data such as headcount with financial data such as payroll, and benchmark.
Must (cybersecurity assurance): assess against the Topical Requirement, using access and patching reports, vendor assurance reports and incident response test results.
Should: prefer evidence obtained directly or from an independent source, and corroborate key points (Standard 14.1).
subtopics.example: Planning a fleet fuel engagement at a Saudi logistics company, internal auditor Reem matches a method to each objective: data analysis of every fuel card transaction against vehicle tank sizes, observation of refueling at two depots, and inspection of the fuel system's user list. Reem records each method and tool in the work program.

review: Compare each planned method with the objective and subject it serves
Inspect cyber steps against the Cybersecurity Topical Requirement's sections
Evaluate whether methods yield first-hand or independent evidence
evidence: Data extraction logs showing the source system and date
Confirmation replies received directly from outside parties
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead check each planned method against the objective it serves before approval.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive, or a supervisor the executive delegates to, approves the methods

subtopics.isaca_rule: Match the method to the subject and the objective, not to habit.

exam_traps.trap: One method, such as interviews, can serve every subject area.
exam_traps.why: Different subjects need different evidence. Interviews build understanding, but finance, IT and cyber objectives usually need records, system data or independent confirmation.

key_terms.definition: Knowledge (ISA 500 A22): a third party's written reply straight to the auditor, on a balance or an agreement's terms and changes.
Knowledge (ISA 500 A28): checking a stated plan against management's record of carrying out past plans, its reasons and its ability.
Comparisons of data, such as ratios, trends and budgets, used to spot unusual results.
Common usage: an independent assurance report on a service provider's controls, which the organization using the service can review.

topics.topic_name: Resources and skills for the engagement
topics.overview: Every engagement needs enough of the right people, money and technology. This topic covers sizing them during planning and what to do when they fall short, from the internal auditor's seat: raise it through the engagement supervisor, and never shrink the work quietly.
can_do: Determine the people, skills, money and technology an engagement needs
Evaluate what a shortfall means for the objectives, the scope and the conclusion
Decide who must hear about a shortfall and which options can close it

subtopics.name: People and Skills for the Engagement
subtopics.definition: Human resources for an engagement are the internal auditors and specialists assigned to it, chosen for the competencies, numbers and availability its tasks need.
subtopics.why_it_matters: An engagement staffed with the wrong skills produces evidence nobody can rely on. Competence is a personal must for each internal auditor and a collective one for the function.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.5): identify the types and quantity of resources needed, weighing the engagement's nature, complexity and time frame.
Should: assign people by the work program's steps and the time each needs, using what the chief audit executive (CAE) knows of staff competencies.
Must (Standard 3.1 Competency): take on only work you have, or can obtain, the competencies for; supervised learning on the job counts.
Must: supervision fits the auditors' experience and the engagement's complexity (Standard 12.3).
May: the CAE adds skills through a guest auditor, an external service provider or another assurance provider (Standard 10.2).
Must: a borrowed expert must be objective; someone from the activity under review cannot test their own area.
subtopics.example: An engagement on a Malaysian palm oil company's carbon credit sales needs carbon market knowledge no internal auditor has. Engagement supervisor Aisyah declines help from the sustainability team that runs the sales and asks the chief audit executive to engage an outside carbon specialist, who works under Aisyah's supervision.

review: Compare the skills each task needs with the assigned team's competencies
Inspect whether guest or outside specialists are free of conflicts
Compare supervisory review hours with the team's seniority mix
evidence: Staffing plan matching tasks to people and hours
Skills matrix or competency records for the assigned team
Objectivity declarations from specialists
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead record which specialist covers each technical task, with an objectivity declaration.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides how missing skills are obtained

subtopics.isaca_rule: Staff the tasks, not the calendar; a needed skill is obtained, never assumed, and never borrowed from the area under review.

exam_traps.trap: Staff from the activity under review can test their own area when internal audit lacks the skill.
exam_traps.why: They are not objective about their own work. The CAE obtains the skill through training, a guest auditor from elsewhere or an outside provider.

key_terms.definition: What an auditor knows and can do, at the level the job needs.
An expert from elsewhere in the organization who joins an engagement to supply a missing skill.

subtopics.name: Money and Technology for the Engagement
subtopics.definition: Financial and technological resources are the budget an engagement draws on, such as hours, travel and specialist fees, and the tools and system access its methods need.
subtopics.why_it_matters: A plan that needs data analysis with no tool, or site visits with no travel budget, cannot reach its objectives. Sizing both early avoids a forced cut to the scope later.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.5): judge whether the money, people and technology on hand are appropriate and sufficient to reach the objectives.
Money covers auditor hours, travel to sites, translation, and fees for outside specialists or tools.
Technology covers data analysis software, access to the activity's systems and data, and secure tools for sharing and storing evidence.
Should: plan the most efficient and effective use of resources; testing a full population with software can beat a large manual sample.
Must (Standard 10.3): the chief audit executive (CAE) trains auditors on new tools and works with IT and information security to set them up.
May: record actual time against budgeted time to improve the next engagement's planning.
subtopics.example: A Kazakh mining group's engagement on equipment maintenance spans six remote sites. Internal auditor Dana budgets hours per site and travel for two visits, and plans to analyze the maintenance system's work orders remotely. The data export needs a tool the team lacks, so Dana tells the engagement supervisor, who arranges the tool, system access and training with the CAE before fieldwork starts.

review: Test the hours budget against the steps and sites in scope
Confirm system access was granted before testing was due
Inspect how evidence files are stored against information security rules
evidence: Approved engagement budget broken down by cost type
Access approvals for the systems and data the tests need
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead request system access and tool licenses as soon as the work program is drafted.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides how money and tools are supplied

subtopics.isaca_rule: Size money and technology from the objectives and the work program's method, and raise a missing tool or budget during planning, not in fieldwork.

exam_traps.trap: The newest analytics tool is always the right technology for an engagement.
exam_traps.why: Technology serves the objectives and the method. A simple test that answers the objective can be more efficient than a new tool the team cannot yet use well.

key_terms.definition: The money an engagement uses, such as auditor hours, travel, translation and outside fees.
The software, devices and system access an engagement's methods need.

subtopics.name: When Resources Fall Short
subtopics.definition: A resource shortfall is a lack of the people, skills, money, time or technology an engagement needs, putting its objectives at risk.
subtopics.why_it_matters: How a shortfall is handled decides whether the conclusion can be trusted; quietly shrinking the work hides a limit the board and management need to know.
how_it_works: Must (Standard 13.5): if resources are inappropriate or insufficient, raise it with the chief audit executive (CAE) to obtain them.
Route: the internal auditor raises it with the engagement supervisor; the supervisor or the CAE discusses it with management of the activity.
Must (Standard 8.2): if resources stay short, the CAE tells the board the impact and how it will be addressed.
Should: the CAE weighs the implications with senior management and the board and chooses the response.
May: the CAE's options include training, a guest auditor, hiring, other assurance providers, rotation with safeguards or outsourcing (Standard 10.2).
Must (Standard 13.3): the CAE approves any scope cut, and the scope must still reach every objective, mandated goals included; a constraint stopping planned work is a scope limitation.
subtopics.example: Two weeks before fieldwork on a Turkish airline's maintenance contracts, the team's only aviation contract expert resigns. Elif, leading the engagement, keeps the technical clauses in scope and raises the gap with the engagement supervisor, who takes it to the CAE and warns the maintenance director of a delay. The CAE arranges a co-sourced specialist and discusses the delay with senior management and the board.

review: Trace each resource gap to its escalation and the decision taken
Compare the final scope with the approved scope for unexplained reductions
Inspect the final communication for any limit the shortfall caused
evidence: Dated escalation note naming the gap and its effect on objectives
Scope change record with reason, approver and date
Board or executive meeting minutes covering the delay
audit_focus.recommend: Have the engagement team lead flag each resource gap the day it appears, with its effect on each objective.
audit_focus.decides: The chief audit executive decides the course of action

subtopics.isaca_rule: Short of resources: raise it, never trim quietly; a cut needs approval and must still reach every objective, and a constraint that stops planned work is a scope limitation.

exam_traps.trap: When staff are short, narrow the scope to what the team can finish and say nothing.
exam_traps.why: A shortfall goes up to the CAE. Any cut must be approved and still reach every objective; a constraint that stops planned work is a scope limitation, discussed with management.

exam_traps.trap: The engagement lead takes a resource shortfall straight to the board.
exam_traps.why: It goes through the engagement supervisor to the CAE, who discusses the implications with senior management and the board.

key_terms.definition: An outside firm or specialist supplying skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.
Sharing engagement work between the internal audit function and an outside provider.

subtopics.memory_aid: Short of resources: tell the chief audit executive, never trim quietly.

key_terminologies.Engagement objectives: What an engagement is meant to establish: its overall aim and the particular results it must deliver.
key_terminologies.Scope: What an engagement will and will not cover.
key_terminologies.Scope limitation: A condition in an assurance engagement, such as restricted access, that prevents the planned work.
key_terminologies.Topical Requirement: A mandatory baseline for assurance engagements on a named subject, such as cybersecurity; recommended for advisory work.
key_terminologies.Applicability assessment: The documented check of each requirement in a Topical Requirement: it applies here, or it is excluded for a stated reason.
key_terminologies.Engagement supervisor: The internal auditor who supervises an engagement: the chief audit executive, or a delegate for whom the chief audit executive stays accountable.
key_terminologies.Criteria: The yardstick for an engagement: what the activity should look like, taken from policy, law, contracts or good practice.
key_terminologies.Condition: What the internal auditors actually found: the existing state of the activity.
key_terminologies.Satisfactory level of control: The share of transactions or controls that must work as intended for a control process to count as acceptable.
key_terminologies.Key performance indicator (KPI): A measure management uses to track progress toward an objective, such as on-time delivery.
key_terminologies.IT general controls: Common usage: controls over the whole IT environment, such as access, change and operations, that every system relies on.
key_terminologies.Business impact analysis: Knowledge (NIST SP 800-34): a study linking a system to the processes it supports and what their disruption would cost.
key_terminologies.Segregation of duties: Dividing a transaction's key steps among different people so that no one can make and hide an error or fraud alone.
key_terminologies.Engagement approach: How an engagement's work is organized and delivered, chosen to fit its objectives, risks and resources.
key_terminologies.Engagement risk assessment: The planning step that identifies and ranks the risks of the activity being examined.
key_terminologies.Pervasive risk: A risk present across an activity or organization, such as fraud or system failure.
key_terminologies.Emerging risk: A new or fast-changing risk with little history, whose likelihood and impact are still uncertain.
key_terminologies.Heat map: A grid plotting risks by likelihood and impact so the most significant stand out.
key_terminologies.Key control: A control that a significant risk mainly depends on.
key_terminologies.Risk and control matrix: A working table that lines up objectives, risks and the controls meant to manage them.
key_terminologies.Design adequacy: Whether a control, performed as written, would keep its risk at an acceptable level.
key_terminologies.Reperformance: The internal auditor carrying out the control again to see whether it gives the right result.
key_terminologies.Work program: The approved list of steps an engagement will perform to meet its objectives.
key_terminologies.Competency: What an auditor knows and can do, at the level the job needs.
key_terminologies.Guest auditor: An expert from elsewhere in the organization who joins an engagement to supply a missing skill.
key_terminologies.External service provider: An outside firm or specialist supplying skills, tools or staff for internal audit work.
